claim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) afflicts approximately 1 in 400 people worldwide.
source: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that afflicts approximately 1 in 400 people worldwide (Alonso et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alonso et al., 2009.

claim: Approximately 10-15% of ALS patients meet formal criteria for a diagnosis of frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: While predominantly a motor disorder, many ALS patients experience cognitive and behavioral changes, and ~10–15% of ALS patients meet formal criteria for a diagnosis of frontotemporal dementia (FTD; Lattante et al., 2015; Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lattante et al., 2015 and Ling et al., 2013.

claim: The C9ORF72 hexanucleotide expansion is the most common genetic cause of co-occurring ALS and FTD.
source: The co-occurrence of ALS and FTD is genetically determined in some cases, most often by the dominantly inherited C9ORF72 (C9) hexanucleotide expansion (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011 and Renton et al., 2011.

claim: The presence of expanded C9ORF72 increases the chance that an ALS patient will be diagnosed with FTD from 10% to approximately 50%.
source: The presence of a single copy of expanded C9 increases sharply the chance that an ALS-afflicted individual will be diagnosed with FTD, from 10 to ~50% (Byrne et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Byrne et al., 2012.

claim: The C9ORF72 repeat-containing RNA can directly sequester the RNA-binding protein hnRNP H, leading to dysregulation of pre-mRNA splicing.
source: we have shown that the repeat-containing RNA can directly sequester the RNA-binding protein (RBP) hnRNP H, leading to dysregulation of pre-mRNA splicing (Conlon et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Conlon et al., 2016).

claim: In almost all ALS and over half of FTD patients, pathological cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 correlates with areas of neurodegeneration.
source: In almost all ALS and over half of FTD patients, the distributions of pathological cytoplasmic accumulation of the hnRNP-like DNA/RNA binding protein TDP-43 tend to correlate with areas of neurodegeneration (Baloh, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baloh, 2011.

claim: The sequestration of hnRNP H altered the splicing of target transcripts in C9ALS patients.
source: Previously, we reported that the sequestration of hnRNP H altered the splicing of target transcripts in C9ALS patients (Conlon et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Conlon et al., 2016).

claim: The hnRNP H splicing signature occurs in half of 50 postmortem sporadic, non-C9 ALS/FTD brains.
source: Here, we show that this signature also occurs in half of 50 postmortem sporadic, non-C9 ALS/FTD brains.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing splicing analysis of 50 sporadic patient brains.

claim: 'Like-C9' sporadic brains contained correspondingly high amounts of insoluble TDP-43.
source: Furthermore, and equally surprisingly, these 'like-C9' brains also contained correspondingly high amounts of insoluble TDP-43, as well as several other disease-related RBPs, and this correlates with widespread global splicing defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 'Like-C9' sporadic brains contained high amounts of several other disease-related RBPs in insoluble form.
source: Furthermore, and equally surprisingly, these 'like-C9' brains also contained correspondingly high amounts of insoluble TDP-43, as well as several other disease-related RBPs, and this correlates with widespread global splicing defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing insolubility of multiple RBPs including FUS, hnRNP A1, and SMN.

claim: High RBP insolubility in 'like-C9' brains correlates with widespread global splicing defects.
source: Furthermore, and equally surprisingly, these 'like-C9' brains also contained correspondingly high amounts of insoluble TDP-43, as well as several other disease-related RBPs, and this correlates with widespread global splicing defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential splicing events correlating with RBP insolubility.

claim: Like-C9 sporadic patients were much more likely to have developed FTD than like-control patients.
source: Finally, we show that the like-C9 sporadic patients, like actual C9ALS patients, were much more likely to have developed FTD.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing like-C9 patients were 3.8 times more likely to have FTD symptoms (p=0.032).

claim: The average percent insoluble hnRNP H was 69.2% in like-C9 patients and 38.9% in like-control patients.
source: Using 39 samples (18 like-control and 21 like-C9), we found that the average percent insoluble hnRNP H was 69.2 in like-C9s, and 38.9 in like-control, or 1.78 times higher in like-C9, a highly significant increase in aggregated protein (p<0.0001) (Figure 2d; all average percent insolubility values are shown by patient in Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Western blot data from biochemical fractionation experiments.

claim: hnRNP H insolubility in like-C9 patients is 1.78 times higher than in like-control patients.
source: Using 39 samples (18 like-control and 21 like-C9), we found that the average percent insoluble hnRNP H was 69.2 in like-C9s, and 38.9 in like-control, or 1.78 times higher in like-C9, a highly significant increase in aggregated protein (p<0.0001) (Figure 2d; all average percent insolubility values are shown by patient in Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of biochemical fractionation data.

claim: The 1.78-fold increase in hnRNP H insolubility in like-C9 sporadic patients closely resembles the 1.9-fold increase previously reported in C9ALS/FTD compared to controls.
source: This enrichment closely resembles the 1.9-fold increase we previously reported in seven C9ALS/FTD (56.1% insoluble) compared to controls (30.0% insoluble).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previously published data from Conlon et al., 2016.

claim: Percent sarkosyl-insoluble hnRNP H correlates with splicing severity (r-square = 0.58).
source: We found that the general trend was for patients with large changes in splicing to have high insoluble hnRNP H (Figure 2e; r-square = 0.58).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: 19 of 26 sporadic ALS/FTD patients with available pathological reports exhibited focal loss of Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum.
source: Reinforcing this view, we also examined available postmortem pathological reports from 26 of the sporadic ALS/FTD patients. Significantly, 19 of these were noted to exhibit focal loss of Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum (Supplementary file 1A), confirming that regions of the brain undergoing robustly measured splicing defects did indeed experience neuronal degeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathological reports documented in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: TDP-43 displays histopathological evidence of cytoplasmic accumulation/aggregation in virtually all ALS cases.
source: For example, as mentioned above, TDP-43 displays histopathological evidence of cytoplasmic accumulation/aggregation in virtually all ALS cases.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'as mentioned above'.

claim: TDP-43 was insoluble at an average of 40.8% in like-C9 patients compared to 5.3% in like-control patients at 21,000 x G fractionation.
source: However, our data present a significant contradiction of this tenet, as 21,000 x G fractionation revealed TDP-43 to be, on average, only 5.3% insoluble in the 10 like-control patients. Meanwhile, 10 patients that were on the same clinical and pathological spectrum yet classified as like-C9 had on average almost eight times as much insoluble TDP-43 (40.8 versus 5.3%, t test p<0.0001) (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Western blot data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Like-C9 patients had almost eight times as much insoluble TDP-43 as like-control patients.
source: Meanwhile, 10 patients that were on the same clinical and pathological spectrum yet classified as like-C9 had on average almost eight times as much insoluble TDP-43 (40.8 versus 5.3%, t test p<0.0001) (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of biochemical fractionation data.

claim: At 180,000 x G fractionation, the majority of TDP-43 was insoluble in like-C9s (68.2%) compared to a minority in like-controls (25.2%).
source: Fractionation of the same samples at 180,000 x G revealed a majority of TDP-43 to be insoluble in like-C9s (68.2%) compared to a minority in like-controls (25.2%; p<0.0001; Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Western blot data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Of 23 sporadic cases with pathological analysis data, only two lacked detectable TDP-43 inclusions in motor regions.
source: Of the 23 sporadic cases for which we possessed data for pathological analysis by immunohistochemistry with TDP-43 antibodies, only two were found to lack detectable TDP-43 inclusions in motor regions (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathological data documented in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Patient F10, the most like-C9 case, lacked detectable TDP-43 inclusions but had an average of 61.8% insoluble TDP-43.
source: One of these, s30, was a like-control case, while the other, F10, was the most like-C9 case (lowest CSS), and had an average of 61.8% insoluble TDP-43 based upon two measurements at 180,000 and 21,000 x G each (Figures 3f and 4i, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data and pathological reports.

claim: Patient 36 had only 2.3% insoluble TDP-43 yet TDP-43 pathology was evident.
source: Conversely, case 36 had only 2.3% insoluble TDP-43 based upon two measurements at 180,000 and 21,000 x G each (Figures 3f and 4i, respectively), yet TDP-43 pathology was indeed evident (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data and pathological reports.

claim: TDP-43 antibody successfully co-immunoprecipitated hnRNP H from sarkosyl insoluble pellets of like-C9 brains.
source: Indeed, TDP-43 antibody successfully co-IPed hnRNP H, while a negative control antibody (FLAG-M2) or beads alone did not (Figure 4l).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4l.

claim: No insoluble FUS could be detected in any like-control patient, while it was present in all like-C9 patients (between 6.1 and 69.1%).
source: Indeed, no insoluble FUS could be detected in any like-control patient, while it was present in all of the like-C9s (between 6.1 and 69.1%).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of biochemical fractionation experiments.

claim: The correlations between CSS and percentage insoluble protein for hnRNP H, TDP-43, FUS and hnRNP A1 each fit remarkably well to a line (r-square = 0.89, 0.79, 0.80 and 0.90, respectively).
source: Intriguingly, we found that the correlations between CSS and percentage insoluble protein for hnRNP H, TDP-43, FUS and hnRNP A1 each fit remarkably well to a line (r-square = 0.89, 0.79. 80 and 0.90, respectively) (Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: GAPDH showed no insoluble protein in any of the 20 cases analyzed.
source: Analysis of GAPDH revealed no insoluble protein in any of the 20 cases (Figure 3e) confirming that insolubility of these RBPs was not due to an artifact of fractionation or global protein insolubility in like-C9s.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: SMN was insoluble in all like-C9 cases with a range from 8.1-61.8% (31.1% on average), but in none of the like-controls.
source: Intriguingly, a fraction of SMN was insoluble in all the like-C9 cases with a range from 8.1–61.8%, or 31.1% on average, but in none of the like-controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of low-speed fractionation experiments.

claim: U2AF65 had low levels of insoluble protein in six of ten like-C9 patients, averaging 9.2%.
source: The non-disease associated proteins (Figure 4f and g) did not display any insolubility, except for U2AF65 (Figure 4h), which had low levels of insoluble protein in six of ten like-C9s, or 9.2% on average (Figure 4i).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4h and quantification in Figure 4i.

claim: Histone H3 and C9ORF72 did not display any insolubility in the analyzed samples.
source: The non-disease associated proteins (Figure 4f and g) did not display any insolubility, except for U2AF65 (Figure 4h), which had low levels of insoluble protein in six of ten like-C9s, or 9.2% on average (Figure 4i).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 4f and 4g.

claim: The top pairwise correlations of RBP insolubility were between hnRNP H and TDP-43 at both 180,000 and 21,000 x G (Spearman r = 0.95 for both).
source: The top pairwise combinations between different proteins were between hnRNP H and TDP-43 at both 180,000 and 21,000 x G (Figure 4k; Spearman r = 0.95 for both).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Fractionation of 13 C9 patients showed correlation between hnRNP H and TDP-43 insolubility (Spearman r = 0.71).
source: Supporting the idea that primary insolubility of hnRNP H can drive insolubility of these other factors, we performed fractionation at 21,000 x G with 13 C9 patients and found similar correlation between hnRNP H and TDP-43 (Spearman r = 0.71) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of fractionation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eight of 18 TDP-43 splicing targets showed changes consistent with TDP-43 loss-of-function in like-C9 patients compared to like-control patients.
source: Using a t-test for each event, and a more permissive cutoff for statistical significance (p<0.10), we found that 10 of the 18 events displayed significant changes. Of these events, eight were as predicted consistent with the like-C9 group having lower concentrations of functional TDP-43, while the other two displayed the opposite trend.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis of TDP-43 splicing targets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The average percentage insoluble hnRNP H was 26.4% in ALSlow, 59.4% in C9, 67.3% in ALShigh, and 79.6% in FTD groups.
source: The average percentage insoluble hnRNP H (180,000 x G) in each group was 26.4 in ALSlow, 59.4 in C9, 67.3 in ALShigh and 79.6 in FTD (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There were no changes in overall hnRNP H abundance in the cerebellum between patient groups.
source: In order to rule out differential hnRNP H levels in the cerebellum of these patients, we performed WB of tissue from 26 of the samples, and observed that there were no changes in overall hnRNP H abundance between these groups (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Comparison of neurologically normal and SOD1 ALS groups found very few (23) detectable splicing differences.
source: To confirm our assumption that neurological normal and SOD1 ALS could be grouped as one, we compared these two groups and indeed found very few (23) detectable splicing differences (|∆PSI| ≥ 0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis using Leafcutter.

claim: ALShigh and C9 groups had 1300-1400 differential splicing events, while the FTD group had several thousand.
source: The paucity of splicing defects in these patients contrasted with 1300–1400 DS events in ALShigh and C9 groups and several thousand in the FTD group (Figure 5d; events listed in Supplementary file 1B), with 488 events overlapping between C9, FTD and ALShigh.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: 488 differential splicing events overlapped between C9, FTD and ALShigh groups.
source: The paucity of splicing defects in these patients contrasted with 1300–1400 DS events in ALShigh and C9 groups and several thousand in the FTD group (Figure 5d; events listed in Supplementary file 1B), with 488 events overlapping between C9, FTD and ALShigh.
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Only 27 or 8% of all differential splicing events detected in C9 were unique to that group.
source: As validation of our like-C9 nomenclature, with or without filtering respectively, only 27 or 8% of all events detected in C9 were unique to that group; the remainder were detected in ALShigh, FTD or both (like-C9 collectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of differential splicing events.

claim: Of C9 differential splicing events, approximately 48% were shared with both ALShigh and FTD, while 40% and 12% were exclusively shared with FTD or ALShigh, respectively.
source: Of the remaining 73% of events that were detected in C9 (with filtering), approximately half (48%) were shared with both other groups, while 40 and 12% of events, respectively, were exclusively shared with FTD or ALShigh (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The ALSlow group had an insignificant number of differential splicing events, even without filtering.
source: Furthermore, the ALSlow group had an insignificant number of events, even without filtering, upholding our definition of like-control for splicing in general.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis.

claim: Differential splicing events affecting RBPs include FUS exon 7, hnRNP A1 exon 8, hnRNP D exon 7 and TIA-1 exon 5.
source: Interestingly, several of the events found to affect RBPs (FUS exon 7, hnRNP A1 exon 8, hnRNP D exon 7 and TIA-1 exon 5) have been the subject of intensive inquiry for their potential roles in disease (Deshaies et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2013) as well regulating splicing and interactions with other hnRNPs (Gueroussov et al., 2017; Izquierdo and Valcárcel, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Increased skipping of MAPT exon 10 was observed in C9, ALShigh and FTD groups.
source: One especially noteworthy example was the increased skipping of MAPT exon 10, observed in C9, ALShigh and FTD (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis.

claim: Genetic mutations in MAPT exon 10 or the surrounding intron are a significant cause of familial FTD.
source: Alternative inclusion of this exon perturbs a delicate balance between 3-repeat and 4-repeat Tau, and genetic mutations in exon 10 or the surrounding intron are a significant cause of familial FTD (Ghetti et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghetti et al., 2015.

claim: Like-C9 patients were 3.8 times more likely to have symptoms of FTD versus like-control patients (p=0.032).
source: We compared these ratios using a Fisher's exact test, and found that like-C9 patients were on average 3.8 times more likely to have symptoms of FTD versus like-control patients (Figure 6e, p=0.032).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: 72% (13/18) of patients with FTD symptoms were classified as like-C9.
source: Of the 50 patients in this analysis, 18 had symptoms of FTD, and were clinically diagnosed with either ALS-FTD or pure FTD, while the remaining 32 patients were diagnosed with ALS without cognitive or behavioral impairment. The majority (13/18; 72%) of the patients characterized by symptoms of FTD were like-C9, while only five of the patients with FTD symptoms were like-control.
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data analysis.

claim: C9 patients are approximately four times more likely than the ALS population at large to receive a diagnosis of FTD.
source: Strikingly, these findings mirror what has been reported for C9 patients, who are approximately four times more likely than the ALS population at large to receive a diagnosis of FTD (Byrne et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Byrne et al., 2012.

claim: TDP-43 pathology is not sufficient to confer detectable splicing differences relative to neurologically normal controls or SOD1 ALS patients.
source: Through stratification of patient samples based on biochemical insolubility of hnRNP H, and by extension TDP-43, we found that TDP-43 pathology is not sufficient to confer detectable splicing differences relative to neurologically normal controls or SOD1 ALS patients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing that like-control patients with TDP-43 pathology had minimal splicing changes.

claim: Biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with splicing defects.
source: our finding that biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with splicing defects as well as with insolubility of several other RBPs casts doubt on the TDP-43-centric view of ALS (Lagier-Tourenne and Cleveland, 2009; Scotter et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TDP-43 insolubility and splicing changes.

claim: Biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with insolubility of several other RBPs.
source: our finding that biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with splicing defects as well as with insolubility of several other RBPs casts doubt on the TDP-43-centric view of ALS (Lagier-Tourenne and Cleveland, 2009; Scotter et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Increased inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7 leads to an isoform with an extended GY-rich region that makes increased contacts with other hnRNPs.
source: In our analysis, we observed increased inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7, leading to an isoform with an extended GY-rich region that makes increased contacts with other hnRNPs, thereby potentially promoting overly stable RBP complexes.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data and inference from previous studies on hnRNP D.

claim: hnRNP A1 exon 8 was more skipped as RBP insolubility increased.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, hnRNP A1 exon 8 was found in our data to be more skipped as RBP insolubility increased, which seems to contradict a recent study suggesting that reduced levels of TDP-43 promote inclusion of this exon (Deshaies et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis.

claim: Reduced levels of soluble FUS lead to increased inclusion of FUS exon 7.
source: In contrast, the loss of soluble FUS, which regulates its own transcript, may explain FUS splicing defects in our data. Normally, FUS protein represses inclusion of exon 7, leading to a FUS isoform that undergoes nonsense-mediated decay in a self-regulating loop (Zhou et al., 2013). Thus, it may be that reduced levels of soluble FUS lead to the observed increase in exon 7 inclusion, thereby resulting in excess levels of FUS that either seed RBP aggregates or 'pile on' to existing ones.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data and inference from previous studies on FUS autoregulation.

claim: FUS protein normally represses inclusion of exon 7, leading to a FUS isoform that undergoes nonsense-mediated decay in a self-regulating loop.
source: Normally, FUS protein represses inclusion of exon 7, leading to a FUS isoform that undergoes nonsense-mediated decay in a self-regulating loop (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: The C9 expansion has been associated with disease incidence in Huntington's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Schizophrenia.
source: Further complicating matters, the C9 expansion has been associated with scarce disease incidence in a wide spectrum of neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions, including Huntington's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Schizophrenia (Hensman Moss et al., 2014; Lesage et al., 2013; McLaughlin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hensman Moss et al., 2014; Lesage et al., 2013; McLaughlin et al., 2017.

claim: Splicing changes affecting EAAT2 were found region-specifically and in most, but not all, sporadic ALS patients 20 years ago.
source: The observation that defects in mRNA splicing may have relevance to ALS was made 20 years ago, through examination of the disease-relevant EAAT2 gene product (Lin et al., 1998). In retrospect, our findings shed new light on the observation that splicing changes could be found region-specifically, and in most, but not all, sporadic patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 1998.

claim: Subtle alterations in SMN concentration cause highly specific degeneration of spinal motor neurons in SMA.
source: The heightened sensitivity of spinal MNs implied by this gradient parallels what is known about SMA, a disease where subtle alterations in the concentration of the protein SMN cause highly specific degeneration of spinal MNs, with further increasing deficiency in SMN resulting in wider systemic dysfunction (Tu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tu et al., 2017.

claim: Disease mechanisms in both ALS/FTD and SMA have been suggested to converge on perturbations of granule dynamics.
source: In both cases, disease mechanisms have been suggested to converge on perturbations of granule dynamics (Zhang et al., 2006; Shan et al., 2010; Ishihara et al., 2013) and RNA splicing (Tsuiji et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2006; Shan et al., 2010; Ishihara et al., 2013; Tsuiji et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: FTD patients displayed the highest hnRNP H insolubility and the most numerous and acute PSI changes.
source: In the above analysis based on solubility groupings, the FTD samples were noteworthy in that they displayed the highest hnRNP H insolubility, as well as the most numerous and acute PSI changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and biochemical fractionation data.

claim: Several sporadic and C9 ALS patients with high insolubility had similar differential splicing patterns to FTD patients.
source: However, several sporadic and C9 ALS patients with high insolubility had similar DS patterns, implying that the excessive events were not somehow specific to the FTD clinical diagnosis, but rather the result of exceptionally high insolubility of RBPs, which occurs at a greater rate in FTD than ALS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data showing similar splicing patterns across patient groups with high RBP insolubility.

claim: Hierarchical clustering based on common differential splicing events grouped patients with similar insolubility measurements close to one another.
source: Using the 489 differential events that were common to all groups (488 common to ALShigh, C9 and FTD, and one common to ALSlow as well) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), patients with similar insolubility measurements were grouped close to one another.
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Clustering of patients based on unique differential splicing events also ordered patients according to insolubility.
source: To further support the hypothesis that all DS events are due to insolubility and not particular clinical distinctions, clustering of patients based on the top events that were unique to each grouping (20 from each ALShigh, C9 and FTD, and all three events in ALSlow) also ordered the patients according to insolubility (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Controls (neurological normal and SOD1) clustered together with patients with the lowest insolubility.
source: Regardless of whether clustering was performed with either the most shared (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) or the most divergent (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) events, the two groups separated by the farthest distance contained almost exactly the same patients, whereas the controls (neurological normal and SOD1) clustered together with the patients with the lowest insolubility, including samples not in the original ALSlow group.
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: hnRNP H and TDP-43 interact in a manner that is largely RNA dependent.
source: Given that TDP-43 and hnRNP H appear to interact (Appocher et al., 2017; Ling et al., 2010; Sephton et al., 2011) in a manner that is largely RNA dependent (Freibaum et al., 2010), it is reasonable to speculate that changes in RNA binding and/or solubility of one might impact the other, leading to more complex patterns of splicing dysregulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Appocher et al., 2017; Ling et al., 2010; Sephton et al., 2011; Freibaum et al., 2010.

claim: TDP-43 and hnRNP H coexist in the same physical aggregates in like-C9 brains.
source: One explanation for the similar degrees of hnRNP H and TDP-43 insolubility in the sporadic and C9 patient brains is that they coexist in the same physical aggregates. To test this hypothesis, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of hnRNP H from eluates of the sarkosyl insoluble pellets of two like-C9 brains using a TDP-43 antibody for IP (see Materials and methods). Indeed, TDP-43 antibody successfully co-IPed hnRNP H, while a negative control antibody (FLAG-M2) or beads alone did not (Figure 4l).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4l.

claim: Aggregates initially seeded by one RBP can recruit other RBPs in a reciprocal relationship.
source: These results support a reciprocal relationship between insolubility of hnRNP H and TDP-43, whereby aggregates initially seeded by one protein can recruit the other, and vice versa.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from co-immunoprecipitation and correlation data.

claim: ALS/FTD should be considered a multiRBP proteinopathy rather than a TDP-43 proteinopathy.
source: Given the decoupling of visible pathology from biochemical insolubility, with only the latter correlated with splicing dysregulation, our results strongly suggest that ALS/FTD should be considered a multiRBP proteinopathy rather than a TDP-43 proteinopathy.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing multiple RBPs are insoluble and correlate with splicing defects.

claim: Splicing changes and insolubility changes may be confined to vulnerable cell types in some patients, diluted in bulk studies by unaffected cell types.
source: For example, splicing and insolubility changes may be confined to only the most vulnerable cell types in patients (sporadic and C9) that were modestly different from control. As a result, changes in splicing or solubility that occur in a minority subpopulation of cells could be diluted in bulk studies by more numerous transcripts derived from unaffected cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential explanations for the observed data.

claim: Detectable splicing changes and highly insoluble protein levels may only become evident in later stages of progressive RBP coalescence.
source: Another interpretation of our data is that detectable splicing changes and highly insoluble protein levels may only become evident in the later stages of a progressive coalescence of RBPs (Lin et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Lin et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015.

claim: Many factors, including disease-causing mutations, are capable of influencing the balance between protein concentrations in different phases over time.
source: Importantly, many factors, including mutations known to cause disease (Kim et al., 2013; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Martinez et al., 2016; Fay et al., 2017; Mackenzie et al., 2017), are capable of influencing the balance between protein concentrations in each phase over time (Ramaswami et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on disease mechanisms.

claim: All ALS/FTD patients fall at varying points beyond a hypothetical 'toxicity boundary' analogous to phase boundaries describing physiological granule formation.
source: Our model (Figure 6—figure supplement 5) proposes that all ALS/FTD patients fall at varying points beyond a hypothetical 'toxicity boundary' that would be analogous to the phase boundaries that describe physiological granule formation (Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015), only unidirectional.
evidence: The claim is based on a proposed model supported by citations to Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015.

claim: The magnitude of imbalance past a toxicity boundary is related to increased abundance of biochemically insoluble protein and decreased levels of functional RBPs, leading to aberrant splicing.
source: The magnitude of this imbalance, or position past a theoretical tipping point, would thus be related to increased abundance of biochemically insoluble protein and decreased levels of functional RBPs, leading to aberrant splicing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed correlations between insolubility and splicing defects.

claim: Inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7 and hnRNP A1 exon 8 causes inclusion of glycine-tyrosine (GY)-rich intrinsically disordered regions in their respective proteins.
source: Notably, two events found to affect the RBPs hnRNP D and hnRNP A1 (exons 7 and 8, respectively) have been shown to cause inclusion of glycine-tyrosine (GY)-rich intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in their respective proteins (Gueroussov et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gueroussov et al., 2017.

claim: The extended GY-rich region in hnRNP D from exon 7 inclusion potentially promotes overly stable RBP complexes.
source: In our analysis, we observed increased inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7, leading to an isoform with an extended GY-rich region that makes increased contacts with other hnRNPs, thereby potentially promoting overly stable RBP complexes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data and knowledge from Gueroussov et al., 2017.

claim: Spinal motor neurons have heightened sensitivity to alterations in granule dynamics compared to cortical neurons.
source: The heightened sensitivity of spinal MNs implied by this gradient parallels what is known about SMA, a disease where subtle alterations in the concentration of the protein SMN cause highly specific degeneration of spinal MNs, with further increasing deficiency in SMN resulting in wider systemic dysfunction (Tu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed gradient of disease severity and comparison to SMA.

claim: FTD patients are further past a hypothetical toxicity boundary than patients with pure ALS.
source: Our results suggest that FTD patients are further past this hypothetical boundary than are patients with pure ALS, as reflected by the highest values of RBP insolubility, and most global splicing changes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing FTD patients have the highest RBP insolubility and most splicing changes.

claim: All FTD patients in the cohort displayed motor neuron loss, but not all ALS patients displayed signs of frontal cortex deterioration.
source: Given that all of the patients in our cohort with FTD also displayed MN loss, but not all ALS patients displayed signs of frontal cortex deterioration, we propose that the distinct neuronal populations affected by this disease spectrum have differential vulnerabilities to the alterations in granule dynamics that define the toxicity boundary.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical data from the patient cohort.

claim: Distinct neuronal populations affected by ALS/FTD have differential vulnerabilities to alterations in granule dynamics.
source: Given that all of the patients in our cohort with FTD also displayed MN loss, but not all ALS patients displayed signs of frontal cortex deterioration, we propose that the distinct neuronal populations affected by this disease spectrum have differential vulnerabilities to the alterations in granule dynamics that define the toxicity boundary.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from clinical observations and the proposed model.
